title: Evaluating Rainwater Harvesting Under Changing Rainfall Scenarios in the South American Dry  Chaco Rangelands
content: Rainwater harvesting sustains livestock production in many drylands, yet its reliability depends on the annual rainfall amount and the size of events. We evaluated how these two rainfall attributes affect water availability in six livestock impoundments (100 m x 50 m) in the South American Dry Chaco. Using a field-validated water storage model, we simulated 100 years for each of five sce-narios combining contrasting annual rainfall amount and maximum event sizes. For each im-poundment, we quantified annual water inputs, average storage, empty days, daily water security, and the minimum wet-season storage required to retain water through the dry season. We found that higher annual rainfall and larger maximum events generally increased water inputs and storage while reducing empty days. At five of six impoundments, large events under median annual rainfall generated similar responses than those under high annual rainfall, highlighting the im-portance of event size. Nevertheless, responses varied substantially among impoundments: under favorable scenarios, end-of-year water security reached 55–84% at five sites but never exceeded 12% at one. Minimum storage thresholds on May 1 (beginning of the dry season) ranged from <1,950 m3 to >5,000 m3 in different impoundments. These findings show that rainfall distribution and im-poundment-specific storage requirements jointly shape livestock water security and can inform anticipatory management during dry periods. We believe that these findings can be useful to the South American Dry Chaco rangelands, but also to other rangelands of the world.
